documents.title: EUGOGO 2021 clinical practice guidelines for medical management of Graves orbitopathy

chunks.content: Thyroid-associated ophthalmopathy (TAO, AKA thyroid eye disease) represents a presumed autoimmune process closely associated with Graves’ disease (GD) . Not a scintilla of convincing evidence to date has been advanced demonstrating that the immunological makeup of individuals with GD and manifesting TAO are fundamentally distinct from those without periocular disease. In fact, many workers in the field advocate the view that all patients with bono fide GD have some measure of TAO, although it might be subclinical in severity. In the past, treatment options for TAO have been limited to relatively nonspecific agents with multiple off-target side effects. Most notable among these are glucocorticoid steroids, administered locally or systemically , . This reliance on medications unproven by adequate placebo-controlled trials and all of which were unapproved for TAO was necessitated by the pervasive uncertainty surrounding root mechanisms underlying TAO. While the molecular events leading to its development remain incompletely understood, the pathology, natural disease course and clinical consequences of TAO have been described in great detail. Understanding its pathogenesis is evolving as more information comes to light. These insights are frequently accomplished by borrowing investigative strategies gathered during the study of other autoimmune diseases. Better definition of disease mechanisms has allowed development of targeted therapies. Thus, the historical reliance on treatments remaining relatively untested can now give way to a more enlightened approach to patient care. In this review, I attempt to describe many of the most consequential discoveries made over the past few decades concerning TAO and leading to currently available therapy. Given its relative brevity, mention of some important studies may have been omitted. Is TAO a local disease or merely a localized manifestation of a systemic process? Striking concordance between the development of TAO and autoimmune thyroid diseases, more commonly with GD and less frequently with Hashimoto’s thyroiditis, strongly suggests that these processes are intimately intertwined. Many investigators exploring the pathogenesis of TAO and caring for patients with the disease focus almost entirely on local orbital processes rather than considering the systemic events that appear to underlie them. The etiologic basis for TAO remains inadequately explored and the vast emphasis of treatment has focused on orbital tissues. Pathological events occurring within the professional immune system may represent more important therapeutic targets, potentially providing more than a treatment “band aid”. These include loss of immune tolerance within both the central (bone marrow and thymus) and peripheral (tolerogenic dendritic cells, regulatory T cells, among others) immune systems. Thus, therapies simply targeting the orbital tissues may succeed in transiently dampening localized manifestations (inflammation, tissue edema, pain, etc) rather than alleviating their root causes. Genetic and acquired factors promoting GD and TAO Identity of instigating factors underlying development of GD and TAO has alluded the scientific community. A genetic basis for disease susceptibility appears to be layered upon as yet uncertain environmental/acquired factor(s). Several genetic signatures remain candidates as the basis for susceptibility to GD. ( , ) Polymorphisms of TSH receptor (TSHR), CTLA-4, CD25, thyroglobulin, HLA-DRβ-Arg74, CD40 and PTPN22 are among these. An open question concerns whether genetic determinants for GD might differ from those for TAO. To date, no convincing evidence has been advanced suggesting that genetic and nongenetic risk factors for the two disease manifestations differ. A recent study demonstrated significant associations between TAO and HLA profiles such as HLAA*01:01, -A*32:01, -B*37:01, -B*39:01, -B*42:01, -C*08:02, C*03:02, DRB1*03:01, DRB1*14:01 and DQB1*02:01.( ) In contrast, HLA-C*04:01, -C*03:04, -C*07:02 and -DRB1*15:02 appear to represent protective alleles. Epigenetic factors could also account for disease development and the heterogeneous presentations of GD and TAO. It remains a mystery why only 10–30% of patients with thyroid-centric GD develop clinically meaningful TAO. Altered methylation of genes encoding TSHR and several T cell (Tc) signaling molecules has been detected in GD, but these patterns do not appear to differ in patients without TAO compared to those with it. ( ) Alternatively, the medley of disease-associated signaling pathways and genes, the expression and activities of which are altered in thyroid and orbital tissues, could ultimately explain whether individual patients with GD manifest TAO. In addition to genetic and epigenetic factors, “psychic triggers” have long been considered as potentially explaining the sudden onset of GD and perhaps TAO ( – ). Specific antecedent events are frequently associated with developing thyroid dysfunction and ocular manifestations. These include physical stress such as serious injury, myocardial infarction and undergoing major surgery. Personal loss and incarceration represent examples of emotional trauma invoked as causative in some patients. Tobacco smoking and large iodine intake can also increase risk. ( – ) Treatment with the anti-CD52 medication, alemtuzumab, for chronic lymphocytic leukemia and multiple sclerosis has been linked to the onset of thyroid autoimmunity, especially GD without or with TAO. ( , ) Thus multiple exogenous factors have been implicated as potentially triggering GD

These include physical stress such as serious injury, myocardial infarction and undergoing major surgery. Personal loss and incarceration represent examples of emotional trauma invoked as causative in some patients. Tobacco smoking and large iodine intake can also increase risk. ( – ) Treatment with the anti-CD52 medication, alemtuzumab, for chronic lymphocytic leukemia and multiple sclerosis has been linked to the onset of thyroid autoimmunity, especially GD without or with TAO. ( , ) Thus multiple exogenous factors have been implicated as potentially triggering GD and TAO. ( , ) Recent interest in selenium as a dietary constituent and its deficiency as an independent risk in GD has led some workers in the field to advocate dietary supplementation in virtually all patients with these diseases. ( , ) Involvement of the professional immune system in TAO Normal immune responses, such as those elicited in host defense against infections, cancer and mechanical/thermal injury, involve a complex interplay between elements of innate immunity (such as monocytes, dendritic cells, basophils, eosinophils, mast cells, Langerhans cells, macrophages, neutrophils and NK cells) and the two major cellular components of adaptive immunity, Tc and B cells (Bc) ( ). Immune reactivity within the TAO orbit resembles that occurring in other autoimmune diseases (such as rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis, etc) and is likely similar or identical to that occurring within the GD thyroid gland. Both Tc and Bc have been implicated convincingly in the development of TAO by virtue of their documented presence in the diseased orbit. Lymphocytes are present, often in high abundance, relatively early in the orbital disease course but may be absent or sparse later in the disease course. They have been partially characterized, but whether a subpopulation within the orbit is antigen specific has yet to be established. ( – ) Effector and regulatory cells of both lineages are among the infiltrating cells in active TAO. Tc and Bc endorse each other as they participate in multiple immune processes. Balance between these cell populations is thought to determine amplitude of disease activity and magnitude of severity. Some of the abnormalities identified in lymphocytes might be attributed to IGF-IR over-expression in both Tc and Bc. ( , ) This IGF-IR over-expression carries functional consequences. Besides lymphocytes, mast cells have also been identified in affected orbital connective tissues and have been shown to interact directly with TAO orbital fibroblasts (GD-OF), altering the patterns of gene expression in those cells. ( – ) Monocytes and their derivatives, including macrophages, can be detected locally in active TAO. In aggregate, these immune cells generate a substantial array of cytokines which in concert with molecules generated by GD-OF, appear to determine the clinical behavior of TAO. They therefore influence greatly the pattern of tissue reactivity and remodeling. In addition to cytokines, several chemokines and chemoattractants promote the infiltration of “second wave” cell participants into the orbit. In theory, some of these could amplify tissue disruption while others might play largely regulatory/reparative roles in these tissues and therefore facilitate and hasten disease resolution. Tc and Bc can engage in cross-talk with GD-OF by virtue of many costimulatory factors and their cognate receptors. Among these are several molecular bridges such as CD40/CD40L (CD154), growth factors and cytokines. These pathways and the signaling they mediate represent candidate therapeutic targets. The putative role of CD40/CD154 playing an important role in GD and TAO derives from the expression pattern of functional CD40 in thyroid epithelium and orbital fibroblasts. ( , ) Cross-talk between Tc and GD-OF can also occur through a variety of cytokine networks. ( , ) These interactions appear to drive inductions of specific genes in TAO. ( , , ) Besides IL-1β, IL-4, IL-6, and TGF-β, IL-17A appears to participate in the development of TAO ( ) through its upregulation of RANTES. Further, genetically driven CD40 overexpression may represent an increased disease susceptibility.( ) Antigen presenting cells in TAO The search for candidate antigen presenting cells (APCs) within the orbit and potentially involved in TAO has included examining multiple cell-types, including monocytes, macrophages and dendritic cells (Dc). Intra-orbital Dc have yet to be detected in TAO. Bc also present antigens ( ) and thus these cells remain candidates once they have infiltrated the orbit. GD-OF were studied for their potential as APCs, dating back to early studies reporting that interferon γ can induce HLA DR expression more robustly in these fibroblasts than those from healthy donors (H-OF) ( ) and that glucocorticoids can attenuate this induction. ( ) Evidence for the thyrotropin receptor playing a role in TAO Thyrotropin receptor (TSHR) represents the central autoantigen in GD. ( ) Activating anti-TSHR autoantibodies are both pathognomonic for GD and specifically drive the characteristic thyroidal disturbances in the disease.

( ) Evidence for the thyrotropin receptor playing a role in TAO Thyrotropin receptor (TSHR) represents the central autoantigen in GD. ( ) Activating anti-TSHR autoantibodies are both pathognomonic for GD and specifically drive the characteristic thyroidal disturbances in the disease. ( ) Parmentier et al ( ) were the first to molecularly clone the TSHR gene. This was followed shortly thereafter by Feliciello et al ( ) who reported identifying TSHR transcripts at extremely low levels in orbital fat. Subsequently TSHR mRNA was detected in multiple fat deposits outside the orbit. ( ) The seemingly ubiquitous expression of TSHR implies the potential for that receptor to play physiological roles throughout the human body. It has been conjectured that abnormal expression of TSHR within the thymus, perhaps genetically determined, may underlie the pathogenesis of GD. ( ) GD-OF were among the first cultured cell types found to express TSHR transcripts peripheral to the thyroid gland. ( ) Further, GD-OF express somewhat higher levels of the receptor than do those detected in H-OF. Subsequent studies revealed that the protein expressed in GD-OF and H-OF is functional since both TSH and GD-IgG can induce specific gene expression (and in CD34 + fibrocytes, which is described later). These include IL-1 receptor antagonist and IL-6. ( , ) The potential role of DNA methylation in determining how orbital fibroblasts respond to TSH was examined recently. ( ) The authors of that report found that DNA methylation of many genes in both H-OF and GD-OF was increased following treatment with M22, a TSHR agonistic monoclonal antibody cloned from a patient with GD. ( ) Among the methylated genes examined was that encoding IGF-IR. Levels of TSHR expression are upregulated by IGF-I. ( ) Besides the induction of cytokine expression, TSH enhances orbital fibroblast proliferation, actions mediated through PI3K and Akt signaling and induction of miR-146 and miR-155. ( ) Insinuation of IGF-IR in the pathogenesis of TAO Relatedness of the IGF-I pathway to thyroid physiology dates back to the experimental observations of Ingbar and colleagues who reported that both insulin and IGF-I could enhance the actions of TSH and GD-IgG on thyroid epithelial cells. ( ) These investigators began to tease apart the intersection of effects on cell proliferation of TSH and IGF-I; however, the details of molecular interplay between the respective signaling pathways had yet to be identified. Later, Weightman and colleagues described the ability of GD-IgG to displace radiolabeled IGF-I from the then unidentified binding sites on the surface of orbital fibroblasts. ( ) That binding site was later identified as IGF-IR and its signaling properties and involvement in responses to GD-IgG were characterized several years thereafter. ( , ) Directly relevant to TAO, GD-IgG was shown to induce the expression of two powerful chemoattractants in GD-OF, namely IL-16 (a CD4-specific ligand) and “regulated upon activation, normal T cell expressed and presumably secreted” (RANTES). Critically, those studies identified the necessary role of IGF-IR in transducing the cellular responses to rhTSH and GD-IgG and the resulting activation of downstream target genes. They brought to light inherent differences in responses elicited in GD-OF compared to H-OF. ( – ) Subsequently, it was determined that the levels of IGF-IR expression in TAO Tc and Bc as well as GD-OF were considerably higher than in those respective cell types derived from healthy individuals. ( , , ) Moreover, abnormal IGF-IR signaling in these cells was found to have functional consequences in each. The importance of β-arrestins in the interactions between IGF-IR and TSHR has illuminated a number of potentially important aspects of pathogenic signaling initiated by autoantibodies in GD and TAO (reviewed recently by Girnita et al ). ( ) Subsequent studies conducted in vitro revealed that IGF-IR inhibition can result in attenuation of responses to TSH, IGF-I and GD-IgG in CD34 + fibrocytes. ( ) Teprotumumab, a fully human IGF-IR-specific monoclonal antibody inhibitor, can attenuate both basal and TSH-dependent expression of Bc activating factor (BAFF), thyroglobulin, TSHR, sodium iodide symporter, thyroperoxidase, and IL-10 in CD34 + fibrocytes. ( ) It can enhance levels of IL-12p35, both intracellular and secreted IL-1 receptor antagonist, and Slit2 while downregulating IL-23p19. The small molecule IGF-IR tyrosine kinase inhibitor, linisitinib, can mimic the effects of teprotumumab. In contrast, teprotumumab fractionally enhances the synthesis of hyaluronan in GD-OF through an upregulation of HAS2 levels. ( ) It can enhance levels of IL-12p35, both intracellular and secreted IL-1 receptor antagonist, and Slit2 while downregulating IL-23p19. The small molecule IGF-IR tyrosine kinase inhibitor, linisitinib, can mimic the effects of teprotumumab. In contrast, teprotumumab fractionally enhances the synthesis of hyaluronan in GD-OF through an upregulation of HAS2 levels. Fibroblasts from the TAO orbit GD-OF, initially characterized by Sisson and colleagues, ( , ) are widely considered the major cellular effectors in the TAO orbit. ( ) Despite substantial evidence to the contrary, GD-OF are frequently considered as monolithic and investigated as representing a homogeneous cell population rather than as a mixture of fibroblastic cells exhibiting substantially divergent phenotypic attributes. ( , ) The vast majority of studies on GD-OF have failed to examine the cellular characteristics of subsetted cells based on specific markers, potentially obscuring the important cellular attributes of each fibroblast subtype. The heterogeneity of GD-OF cultures was initially found to comprise both Thy-1 + (AKA CD90) and Thy-1 − cells displaying similar morphologies and growth characteristics. ( ) Soon thereafter, initial attempts at studying pure cell subsets of primary cultures yielded insights into the divergent capacities of Thy-1 + and Thy-1 − cells to undergo differentiation. The Thy-1 + phenotype possesses the capacity to differentiate into myofibroblasts when exposed to TGF-β. In contrast, Thy-1 − GD-OF more readily differentiate into adipocytes when activated through the proliferator-activated receptor γ pathway. ( , ) Thus, it would appear that GD-OF represent a heterogeneous population of cells based on Thy-1 surface display and that this heterogeneity carries functional and disease susceptibility implications. Emergence of CD34<sup>+</sup> fibrocyte involvement in TAO and comprising GD-OF subpopulations An additional cellular characteristic, the basis of which allowed further segregation of mixed populations of GD-OF, emerged following identification of CD34 + CXCR4 + Collagen 1 + cells in the parental strains of GD-OF. ( ) These cells appear to represent infiltrating CD34 + fibrocytes that masquerade in the TAO orbit as cells morphologically similar to residential CD34 − OF. ( ) Fibrocytes have an established role in tissue remodeling, fibrosis and wound healing. ( ) They have been implicated in multiple autoimmune diseases including scleroderma and rheumatoid arthritis. ( ) These cells can efficiently present antigens to Tc by virtue of their display of B7 costimulatory molecules and MHC II. ( ) They can be readily identified by their retention of molecular markers including CD34, CXCR4 and collagen 1. Like their putative progenitors, circulating fibrocytes coming from the bone marrow, they express relatively high levels of TSHR, establishing their potential relevance in TAO and GD. ( ) In addition to TSHR, fibrocytes express thyroperoxidase, functional thyroglobulin, and sodium iodide symporter. ( , ) The expression of these proteins by fibrocytes seems to rely on the autoimmune regulator protein (AIRE), a noncanonical transcription factor involved in thymic Tc education. Interrogation of CD34 + OF have revealed that these cells, like fibrocytes, also express thyroid-associated molecules but at substantially lower levels of protein and encoding mRNAs. It appears that once these cells infiltrate the orbit and become tissue cohabitants with CD34 − OF, their switching from high to low level expression of these molecules is the consequence, at least in part, of Slit2 coming from CD34 − OF. Slit2 appears to downregulate specific gene expression at both the transcriptional and post-transcriptional levels. ( ) An as yet unresolved issue concerns whether endogenous or extrinsic factors determine whether fibrocytes contribute to the development of TAO, either as effectors (promoting disease) or as players with a largely regulatory role (dampening disease). Circulating fibrocytes from patients manifesting TAO express higher levels of TSHR than do those from healthy individuals and those with GD but without TAO. CD34 + fibrocytes have substantial capacity for presenting antigens in a variety of physiological and pathological contexts. ( ) This is likely true while they are infiltrating tissue niches or in circulation. Thus, fibrocytes may represent an important component of immune response in TAO. Slit2, an enforcer of fibrocyte civility and molecular tranquility? Slit2, a neuronal axon repellent glycoprotein, is expressed and released from CD34 − OF. It was first identified for its importance in enforcing midline integrity during CNS development. ( ) Slit2 has been shown to inhibit fibrocyte differentiation, thereby modulating fibrosis in lung tissue. ( ) It acts through its cognate receptor, roundabout 1 (ROBO1).( ) CD34 + fibrocytes express ROBO1 and when engaged by Slit2, this receptor is activated, resulting in down regulation of TSHR, Tg, TPO, and NIS levels. Slit2, a neuronal axon repellent glycoprotein, is expressed and released from CD34 − OF. It was first identified for its importance in enforcing midline integrity during CNS development. ( ) Slit2 has been shown to inhibit fibrocyte differentiation, thereby modulating fibrosis in lung tissue. ( ) It acts through its cognate receptor, roundabout 1 (ROBO1).( ) CD34 + fibrocytes express ROBO1 and when engaged by Slit2, this receptor is activated, resulting in down regulation of TSHR, Tg, TPO, and NIS levels. ( ) These inhibitory effects on gene expression are apparently mediated through the downregulation of AIRE. In addition, Slit2 enhances IL-12 expression while attenuating that of IL-23 through action on gene transcription levels. ( ) Slit2 upregulates HAS2, increasing the production of hyaluronan in GD-OFs. ( ) Thus, Slit2 appears to support HA synthesis in certain cell types. Current therapeutic landscape for TAO: an expanding role for medical intervention? Given the broadening insights into TAO pathogenesis, several candidate molecular targets for medical intervention have been identified recently, based on experimental inquiry leading to increased plausibility ( ). Thus, for the first time, targeted therapy has emerged from near-complete reliance on nonspecific agents. As mentioned earlier, the majority of nonsurgical therapy for TAO, specifically timed during the inflammatory, progressive phase, has involved use of either local or systemic glucocorticoid steroids. ( ) Considerable debate continues to rage over the wisdom of continuing the use of steroids in light of newer, more targeted agents. ( ) While several European experts have long advocated steroids as the “gold standard” medical therapy, recent evidence indicates that the majority of North American physicians treating TAO do not use these agents routinely. ( ) Further, only a single trial, involving 15 patients with moderate to severe TAO, has been reported as placebo controlled. The authors of that study ( ) concluded steroid superiority over placebo based on responses heavily weighted toward inflammation-related signs and symptoms over 48-week observation. Methylprednisolone (6g total) was administered over 3 months in 6 patients compared with 9 patients receiving placebo. Importantly, response in reducing proptosis and improving diplopia was not essential for achieving primary response in this study. A more recent approach, based on a single published trial not reaching its primary endpoint, concluded that the combination of high-dosage pulse steroids and mycophenolate might be superior to steroids as single agents. ( ) Remarkably, this combination therapy has been touted as “first line” therapy for moderate-to-severe TAO in the recently published EUGOGO guidelines. ( ) The recommendation has been challenged based on the inadequate evidence supporting its use. ( ) A statement including mycophenolate as first line therapy for TED is not included in the even more recently published joint statement from the European-American Thyroid Association. ( ) Birth of teprotumumab for the treatment of TAO Teprotumumab, a fully human IgG1 monoclonal antibody IGF-IR inhibitor, was developed by Roche as a therapy for solid cancers. The program at Roche was paralleled by those of several other pharmaceutical companies, each with their own molecule targeting IGF-IR. After outcomes of several clinical trials were analyzed, these developmental programs were curtailed for lack of efficacy, including that of teprotumumab. Importantly, these studies of IGF-IR inhibitors for cancer, conducted in the 2000’s, ( ) revealed that these drugs were generally well-tolerated with encouraging safety profiles. Teprotumumab was evaluated in two placebo-controlled, double masked, multi- institutional clinical trials in adult patients (18–80 years) with TAO judged to manifest active, short-duration (<9 mos from development) and moderate to severe disease. ( , ) Unlike the standards usually adhered to in judging responses to steroids and other anti-inflammatory agents in TAO, those two studies of teprotumumab included a necessary reduction in proptosis ≥ 2mm in the more seriously affected eye to reach primary response. In addition, improvement in diplopia was also widely observed. More detailed accounting of these clinical responses can be found in recent primary reports and reviews found elsewhere ( , – ) and in other contributions to this collection of papers (Strianese and Pakdel). Several adverse events had emerged from the two clinical trials of teprotumumab, notably including hyperglycemia and auditory abnormalities. It should be anticipated that glucose excursions would occur in patients treated with an IGF-IR inhibitor, given the role of IGF-IR in maintaining normal glucose metabolism. Hyperglycemia developing as the consequence of treatment with teprotumumab has been attributed to several different mechanisms including alterations in gluconeogenesis ( ) and the physical and functional associations occurring between IGF-IR and insulin receptors. ( , ) In fact, most insulin receptor molecules exist as chimeric proteins, associating with IGF-IR. Because these two “half-receptors” interplay functionally, inhibiting IGF-IR most likely results in relative insulin resistance. These and other AEs have been described in detail previously. ( ) Mechanisms involved in clinical responses to teprotumumab <italic toggle="yes">in vivo</italic> The question of how and in which tissues clinically consequential IGF-IR inhibition might be occurring in mediating responses to teprotumumab remains uncertain. Within the orbit, GD-OF express IGF-IR in a physical and functional complex with TSHR in situ .( ) A stimulating TSHR antibody induces IGF-1R phosphorylation and can initiate both TSHR and IGF-1R signaling in fibroblasts from “mice and men”. 1H7, a murine IGF-IR inhibitor monoclonal antibody was found to inhibit multiple IGF-IR signaling cascades and reduce TSHR signaling. ( ) A recent study demonstrated that inhibiting IGF-IR in GD-OF in vitro resulted in “suppressing IGF-1R signaling leading to retro-orbital fibroblast/adipocyte death through the cell-extrinsic pathway of apoptosis”. ( ) That report demonstrated that IGF-IR inhibition can suppress several proteins, including Beclin1, LC3a, LC3b, p62, and ULK1 in GD-OF, all related to autophagy while inducing apoptosis-related proteins, including caspase 3 activation, FADD, and caspase 8. Further the authors state that “This is likely the major mechanism involved in proptosis reduction in patients with Graves’ eye disease treated by IGF-1R inhibition”. ( )Their conclusions may be correct, given the earlier studies demonstrating direct effects of IGF-IR inhibition (1H7, teprotumumab, lisitinib) on GD-OF and CD34 + fibrocytes, but the authors failed to consider information provided in another study which has revealed a very different possibility. That report, by Fernando et al ( ) demonstrated consequences of in vivo actions of teprotumumab in patients treated with teprotumumab. Flow cytometric analysis of peripheral blood mononuclear cells from treated patients with moderate to severe TAO, collected at baseline and following treatment per study protocol ( ) with teprotumumab over 24 weeks, demonstrated substantial reductions in cell surface displayed CD80/CD86, PD-L1, and MHC II levels in CD34 + CXCR4 + fibrocytes. These attenuated protein levels were significant when compared to baseline in paired analysis (p<0.0001). In contrast, levels of these molecules in placebo-treated patients failed to undergo change. Analysis of CD4 + Tc from patients receiving teprotumumab also revealed substantial reductions in IL-17A and IFNγ levels in vivo . Companion studies conducted in vitro disclosed that the effects of teprotumumab were mediated at both transcriptional and mRNA stability. Importantly, IGF-IR inhibition and Slit2 share several consequences, suggesting the possibility that teprotumumab, and perhaps other IGF-IR inhibitors, might act through intermediate effects on endogenous Slit2 activity. In fact, Slit2 and ROBO1, its cognate receptor, were found to be upregulated by teprotumumab in GD-OF. ( ) Potential for increasingly more effective TAO therapies Like virtually all medical therapies for vexing, complex diseases, despite the impressive and unprecedented clinical responses to teprotumumab and the generally well-tolerated attributes of that drug, ineffectiveness in some patients and relatively infrequent side effects invite further treatment improvements. Recent consensus guidance has been provided by a group of ophthalmologists who treat TAO. ( ) Clearly those experts consider use of teprotumumab in a subset of patients to be appropriate. As they and others have noted, the drug is associated with side effects and some patients fail to respond adequately to the 8-infusion treatment protocol frequently employed. Thus, that realization has provoked an ongoing quest for perfection. Multiple molecules targeting IGF-IR are under development and additional therapeutic targets are being considered. Among these are VRDN (another anti-IGF-IR monoclonal antibody) and linisitinib, a small molecule tyrosine kinase inhibitor. Among the more promising and plausible of the alternative therapeutic targets is TSHR, the blockade of which in theory could directly treat the thyroid glandular hyperactivity frequently accompanying GD as well as TAO ( ). Development of molecules acting at TSHR continue. Both monoclonal antibodies and small molecules are currently in the developmental pipeline. ( , ) Another potential target is the CD40/CD154 pathway. more promising and plausible of the alternative therapeutic targets is TSHR, the blockade of which in theory could directly treat the thyroid glandular hyperactivity frequently accompanying GD as well as TAO ( ). Development of molecules acting at TSHR continue. Both monoclonal antibodies and small molecules are currently in the developmental pipeline. ( , ) Another potential target is the CD40/CD154 pathway. This molecular bridge functions in the crosstalk occurring between Tc and Bc and with GD-OF. CD40/CD154 (CD40 ligand) has been therapeutically targeted in other autoimmune diseases. By virtue of their high level CD40 expression, both GD-OF and thyroid epithelial cells can respond to CD154 with induction of IL-6, IL-8, prostaglandin endoperoxide H synthase 2 expression and hyaluronan synthesis. CFZ533, an anti-CD40 blocking monoclonal antibody ( ), was tested in a clinical trial of hyperthyroid patients with GD. Nearly 50% of patients treated with the molecule responded by becoming biochemical euthyroid. ( ) Tocilizumab is a blocking monoclonal antibody directed against the IL-6 receptor and has found a niche in the treatment paradigm of several autoimmune diseases including rheumatoid arthritis (RA), giant cell arteritis, and polyarticular and systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis. ( ) Satralizumab also targets the IL-6 receptor and was recently approved by the FDA for the treatment of neuromyelitis optica. ( ) Tocilizumab has been evaluated recently, primarily in studies centered in Spain in patients resistant to steroids. ( ) Whether IL-6 receptor blockade can result in clinically meaningful reduction of proptosis and/or diplopia in TAO remains uncertain. Critical in the regulation of circulating serum albumin levels and immunoglobulin clearance is the neonatal fragment crystallizable receptor (FcRn). It links these molecules to the lysosomal pathways. Disrupting FcRn-IgG interactions by therapeutically targeting the receptor with monoclonal antibodies can accelerate disposal of pathogenic autoantibodies. Myasthenia gravis is among the diseases for which this approach has been taken. RVT-1401 and HBM9161 represent two monoclonal antibodies thus far being explored for the treatment of GD and TAO. Potential drawbacks to this therapeutic approach include its relative non-specificity and its entire focus on autoantibodies, potentially without altering the pathogenic roles of Tc in these diseases. The trial of RTV-1401, developed by Immunovant, was suspended after reports of drug-related hypercholesterolemia appeared. As of this writing, the trial of RTV-1401 has been restarted. It is thus clear that several strategies are under development for the treatment of TAO. Many appear to possess substantial plausibility based on known disease mechanisms but virtually all can also be associated with concerning adverse events. Recognition of the important signaling pathways and genes expressed by GD-OF and CD34+ fibrocytes has allowed several additional therapeutic targets to be considered. In my view, our ultimate goal should include the restoration of immune tolerance to pathogenic autoantigens underlying TAO. It is very possible that some of these antigenic molecules may remain unidentified. This aspirational goal in theory would spare patients exposure to medications impairing host defense against infections and cancer. Besides developing additional therapies, several other goals must be achieved. Predictive biomarkers are needed to stratify patients according to their risk for developing severe disease, identifying patients more likely to benefit from targeted therapy, and judging therapeutic responses. To date, no molecular signatures reliably delineate those patients with GD who are destined to develop TAO in the future.

documents.title: EUGOGO management of mild Graves orbitopathy consensus

chunks.content: I. Introduction Thyroid eye disease (TED, a.k.a thyroid-associated ophthalmopathy) is an autoimmune condition where connective tissues of the orbit become inflamed and remodeled ( ). It is most frequently associated with Graves’ disease (GD), having an estimated prevalence of 40% among patients with GD ( , ). Up to 8% of cases of TED present without detectable thyroid gland abnormalities ( ). The pathophysiology of TED appears to be driven, at least in part, by autoantibodies against the TSH receptor (TSHR) and perhaps those targeting the insulin-like growth factor I receptor (IGF-IR), leading to structural and functional changes in tissues of the orbit. These tissues are infiltrated by T cells, fibrocytes, macrophages, and other myeloid cells ( ). Besides TSHR, (IGF-IR has been implicated in the disease process ( , ). TED is the most common cause of proptosis in adults ( ). In addition, it can be accompanied by multiple signs and symptoms including lagophthalmos, ocular pain, and double vision. Lacrimal symptoms are commonly experienced in TED, frequently associated with dry eyes, increased (ineffective) tearing, and foreign body sensation. Despite the prevalence of TED, its lacrimal symptoms are frequently misdiagnosed as dry eye syndrome, chronic conjunctivitis, or allergies ( , ). Here we review the relevant literature concerning lacrimal manifestations of TED and their management. Further, we identify current gaps in understanding how the lacrimal system becomes involved in the pathogenesis of TED and suggest potentially productive directions for future investigations. II. Background Pathophysiology The pathophysiology of lacrimal system involvement in TED appears multifactorial. In that disease process, lacrimal glands can become infiltrated by immune cells such as T cells, B cells and monocyte-lineage cells, thus driving an inflammatory response ( ). Th17 cells secreting IL-17A play roles in tissue remodeling by activating pathways mediating fibrosis and adipogenesis ( ). IGF-IR is hypothesized as playing a pivotal role in orbit fibroblast responses occurring in TED though mechanisms remaining incompletely understood ( ). Compared to those in healthy individuals, lacrimal glands in TED express elevated levels of several cytokines including IL-10, IL-12, IL-13, IL-6 and TNF-α ( ). Recent proteomic studies have identified many of these same cytokines in the tear film ( ). Lacrimal gland enlargement can occur, the consequence of inflammation and tissue remodeling ( ). In late-stage TED, lacrimal glands can stiffen and become smaller ( ). Besides factors directly driving lacrimal gland pathology, others may also underly lacrimal symptoms. Anatomical and functional changes in the TED orbit, such as lagophthalmos and proptosis, can result in incomplete blinking ( ). Increased corneal surface exposure can adversely impact lacrimal gland dysfunction. Lacrimal Symptoms in TED Lacrimal symptoms associated with TED include dry eyes, excessive tearing, sensations of grittiness, pain, and photophobia ( ). Dry eyes are a major component of TED, contributing to symptomatology and diminished quality of life (QoL). The Tear Film & Ocular Surface Society (TFOS), a global consortium of researchers, launched the TFOS Dry Eye Workshop II (TFOS DEWS II) in March 2015 to achieve global evidence-based consensus on dry eye disease (DED) ( ). Their definition of DED is as follows: “Dry eye is a multifactorial disease of the ocular surface characterized by a loss of homeostasis of the tear film, and accompanied by ocular symptoms, in which tear film instability and hyperosmolarity, ocular surface inflammation, damage, and neurosensory abnormalities play etiological roles” ( ). Their framework further proposes an etiological continuum of DED ranging from aqueous deficient dry eye (ADDE) to evaporative dry eye (EDE) ( ). In the TFOS DEWS II framework, TED is most directly associated with aqueous deficient dry eye, where lacrimal gland dysfunction disrupts tear film homeostasis and can lead to ocular surface inflammation ( ); however, evaporative factors likely also play a role with increased corneal surface exposure from lid dysfunction ( ). The diagnosis requires both patient experiencing symptoms and manifesting physical signs for DED ( ). One study focusing on TED found that more than two thirds of patients develop both subjective and objective signs of DED ( ). Another report indicated that the most frequent symptoms are dry eye or grittiness, occurring in 57% of patients, ocular pain in 54%, photophobia in 48%, and excessive tearing in 48%. These symptoms often persist over an extended duration (years) ( ). They are frequently accompanied by lid retraction, periocular inflammation, chemosis, proptosis, and lagophthalmos ( ). While proptosis, lid retraction and other manifestations of TED are not directly related to the lacrimal gland system, they can increase eye surface exposure and alter eyelid dynamics, thus worsening lacrimal gland-related symptoms. A link between DED and thyroid dysfunction has been debated ( ). Some studies propose that autoimmune thyroid diseases may contribute to dry eye through lacrimal gland dysfunction ( ); however, evidence remains inconsistent. Yu et al. found

They are frequently accompanied by lid retraction, periocular inflammation, chemosis, proptosis, and lagophthalmos ( ). While proptosis, lid retraction and other manifestations of TED are not directly related to the lacrimal gland system, they can increase eye surface exposure and alter eyelid dynamics, thus worsening lacrimal gland-related symptoms. A link between DED and thyroid dysfunction has been debated ( ). Some studies propose that autoimmune thyroid diseases may contribute to dry eye through lacrimal gland dysfunction ( ); however, evidence remains inconsistent. Yu et al. found no significant association between DED and thyroid gland abnormalities ( ). Conversely, other studies have observed an increased prevalence of DED among patients with a history of thyroid disease ( – ). In sum, any relationship between DED and abnormalities in thyroid function remain uncertain, perhaps attributable to the relatively common nature of both conditions. Impact on QoL Patients with TED report a reduction in their QoL ( ). The periocular manifestations of GD are associated with occupational disability, with one study identifying 36% of patients who took sick leave due to TED, 28% were disabled, 5% retired early, and 3% who had lost their jobs ( ). Activities such as reading, driving, socializing and employment are frequently limited in these patients ( , – ). Few studies have directly quantified the rank-order impact of specific symptoms on QoL in TED. Respondents from one survey reported that dry/gritty eyes are among the most bothersome ( ). This was followed by light sensitivity, bulging eyes, ocular pain/pressure, and excessive tearing. Close observation and treatment of lacrimal symptoms may improve QoL. Clinical Evaluation TED treatment decisions are typically based on clinical activity, severity, and disease duration. The 2021 EUGOGO clinical practice guidelines for medical management recommend using the clinical activity score (CAS) system to assess disease activity ( , ). EUGOGO severity classification stratifies the disease as mild, moderate-to-severe, and sight-threatening. Manifestations such as proptosis and diplopia determine severity while sight-threatening TED can result from anterior eye surface deterioration or compressive optic neuropathy. Other scoring systems have been devised, including VISA, NOSPECS, and total eye scores which allow component quantification ( – ). None of these appears to be widely adopted for routine clinical practice. During treatment, the GO-QOL questionnaire is recommended for primary outcome assessment as well as for routine use in clinical practice ( , , ). Alternatively, when the details of GO-QoL prove too time-consuming, TED-QoL can be a less cumbersome alternative, especially in mild disease ( ). III. Therapeutic Strategies A. Treating elevated thyroid hormone levels Management options for lacrimal-associated symptoms in GD are limited. Much of this small “toolbox” results from our lack of detailed understanding concerning the complex interplay between immune function/dysfunction and the lacrimal system. Normalization of thyroid function and returning patients to the euthyroid state are not conclusively associated with improving lacrimal function ( , ). Of note, lacrimal gland dysfunction can be identified in patients with thyroid cancer who have undergone radioactive iodine ablation of the gland ( ). The direct impact of thyroid hormones on the orbital contents is poorly understood, particularly as it relates to lacrimal system dysfunction in GD and TED. Several basic studies have been conducted on the Harderian gland in non-primate mammals. Harderian glands are absent in human beings but provide some overlapping functions with lacrimal glands in rodents. Reduced lacrimal gland weight was observed in hypothyroid rats, but those tissues express elevated thyroid hormone receptor β1 levels ( ). Both methimazole and propylthiouracil are used to treat hyperthyroidism occurring in GD. They can control glandular overactivity and elevated hormone synthesis ( ). ( ). Evidence suggests that the course of TED is affected by thyroid disfunction and that its optimal management can make an optimal disease outcome more likely ( – ). Hyperthyroidism resulting in thyrotoxicosis, TED, and dermopathy typically exhibit independent clinical courses in GD. Thus, treating thyroid gland dysfunction alone is inadequate for the management of TED, including manifestations directly attributable to the lacrimal system and DED ( ). Importantly, no controlled studies have demonstrated improved outcomes of TED or its shortened duration as a consequence of restoring the euthyroid state to hyperthyroid patients with GD. B. Selenium Supplementation The trace element, selenium, may be therapeutically useful in GD and TED because of its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties ( ). The 2021 EUGOGO clinical guidelines recommend oral selenium supplementation for mild TED (200 μg daily for 6 months) ( ). The scientific evidence for its effectiveness is relatively weak and may be limited to patients in selenium-depleted geographic regions ( , ). The National Academies of Science and Medicine have recommended daily intake ranging from 55 to 70 mcg for adults and 15 to 70

consequence of restoring the euthyroid state to hyperthyroid patients with GD. B. Selenium Supplementation The trace element, selenium, may be therapeutically useful in GD and TED because of its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties ( ). The 2021 EUGOGO clinical guidelines recommend oral selenium supplementation for mild TED (200 μg daily for 6 months) ( ). The scientific evidence for its effectiveness is relatively weak and may be limited to patients in selenium-depleted geographic regions ( , ). The National Academies of Science and Medicine have recommended daily intake ranging from 55 to 70 mcg for adults and 15 to 70 mcg for children and adolescents ( ) In a recent meta-analysis (n = 4), patients receiving selenium supplementation exhibited a significant decrease in palpebral aperture and other non-lacrimal related improvements in disease severity, thereby reducing corneal surface exposure ( ). No statistically significant differences could be identified in adverse event frequency or disease severity between the selenium receiving groups compared with those receiving placebo ( ). Another study examined the longitudinal effects of 6-month selenium supplementation, finding early alleviation of ocular symptoms and signs (i.e. tearing, foreign body sensation, proptosis) but found no differences versus placebo in improvement at 5-year follow-up ( ). Excess selenium supplementation ( ≥ 200 μg/daily for long periods of time) has been associated with selenosis, alopecia, dermatitis, non-melanoma skin cancer, increased mortality, type 2 diabetes, and increased prostate cancer risk ( ). Geographically, selenium deficiency is rare in the United States and Canada but is more widespread in China, New Zealand, parts of Europe, and Russia ( ). A recent RCT studied its supplementation in selenium-sufficient areas (such as South Korea) and found no significant QoL improvement at 6 months. Greater proptosis reduction with selenium was identified at 3 months but this improvement failed to be sustained at 6 months ( ). Further studies substantiating the long-term efficacy and safety of oral selenium supplementation are needed, both in patients living in selenium sufficient and deficient geographic regions. C. Glucocorticoids Systemic methylprednisolone and prednisone Methylprednisolone and prednisone act systemically as corticosteroids. Historically, they have been considered the first-line medical treatment for moderate-to-severe and active TED, although they are not approved for use in TED by the US FDA. Thay can be administered intravenously or orally although intravenous administration is preferred ( ). The hypothesized benefit derived from corticosteroids comes from its generalized immunosuppressive properties. These lessen orbital and periorbital inflammation, including chemosis and edema, which can improve ocular surface symptoms. Therapy with methylprednisolone has improved outcomes including reduced diplopia and better eye motility in several studies, although these studies lacked stringent controls ( ). Evidence for the impact of steroids specifically on the lacrimal symptoms of TED is limited. One prospective study showed significantly reduced levels of cytokines in tear film following high dose methylprednisolone, congruent with improved clinical parameters ( ). Xu et al. found that methylprednisolone therapy administered over 12 weeks significantly reduced the OSD index, presumptively by reducing levels of multiple inflammatory mediators ( ). IV steroids may lower CAS scores more effectively than those taken orally ( ). CAS scores were reduced more effectively with daily corticosteroid dosing than those administered weekly ( ). Further studies are required before assessment of the clinical impact of systemic steroids on lacrimal symptoms such as dry eye, tearing, and photophobia can be made. Triamcinolone Triamcinolone, another corticosteroid, is also used off-label in TED ( , ). Triamcinolone can be administered orally, topically or injected locally, either by periocular or subconjunctival injection. A meta-analysis of 6 studies of triamcinolone efficacy suggests that it may be helpful in reducing eyelid retraction ( ). Thus, locally administered triamcinolone may reduce corneal exposure by lessening eyelid retraction. Further studies will be required to determine whether the drug is effective and safe for this indication. Betamethasone Betamethasone exhibits greater anti-inflammatory effects with longer duration than the aforementioned corticosteroids ( ). In two RCTs, reduction of eyelid retraction with betamethasone was compared to that following triamcinolone ( , ). In one study, patients did not exhibit proptosis. Treatment was considered effective if marginal reflex distance 1 (MRD1) was normalized (≤ 4.5 mm) ( ). Betamethasone injections were effective in 92.9% of patients with a mean number of required injections of 1.61 ± 0.50. In contrast, triamcinolone injections were effective in 60.7% of patients with a mean number of 2.36 ± 1.16 ( ). In another study, efficacy of betamethasone was assessed in patients with proptosis ( ). Treatment was considered effective if MRD1 ≤ 4.5 mm and Hertel ≤ 18 mm. Betamethasone injections were effective in 89.74% of patients. In contrast, 2.54 ± 0.51 triamcinolone injections were necessary and achieved effectiveness in 57.9% of patients (3.74 ± 1.18 injections). In another study, efficacy of betamethasone was assessed in patients with proptosis ( ). Treatment was considered effective if MRD1 ≤ 4.5 mm and Hertel ≤ 18 mm. Betamethasone injections were effective in 89.74% of patients. In contrast, 2.54 ± 0.51 triamcinolone injections were necessary and achieved effectiveness in 57.9% of patients (3.74 ± 1.18 injections). IOP spikes were reported in both treatment groups (2 cases in the betamethasone-treated group, 4 cases in triamcinolone group). Subconjunctival hemorrhage and lid ecchymosis was reported in four patients (2 cases in each treatment group) ( ). Lid crease/sulcus changes or recurrence of eyelid retraction were not detected during the 6-to-20-month follow-up in either study. Thus, betamethasone may be more effective and require fewer injections than triamcinolone. Larger studies with longer follow-up periods will be necessary before any conclusions can be drawn regarding betamethasone as an effective and safe treatment for this indication. D. Biological and Immunosuppressive Agents In recent years, targeted immunosuppressive agents, either biological or small molecule, have emerged as promising therapeutic agents for the management of TED and its lacrimal-related symptoms ( ). Recent studies have demonstrated that TSH receptor (TSHR) and IGF-1 receptor (IGF-1R) form a receptor–receptor signaling complex ( ). Confocal imaging and co-immunoprecipitation demonstrate physical interactions between TSHR and IGF-1R ( , ). Teprotumumab Teprotumumab is a fully human inhibitory monoclonal antibody targeting IGF-IR. The receptor is overexpressed in multiple cell types in GD and TED, including orbital fibroblasts, CD34 + fibrocytes, orbital fibroblasts, B cells and T cells ( – ). Teprotumumab is the first and remains the only FDA-approved treatment for TED ( , ). Its safety and efficacy have been evaluated in five registered clinical trials and 99-week follow-up ( , – ). Diplopia improvement was reported in 73% and proptosis response in 68% ( ). In a prospective longitudinal study, change in lacrimal gland volume and aqueous tear production was assessed in patients (n = 20) receiving 8 teprotumumab infusions over 24 weeks (every three week infusions) (10 mg/kg for the first infusion and 20 mg/kg for subsequent infusions) ( ). The mean lacrimal gland volume of the study orbit (the more severely proptotic eye) decreased from 768 mm 3 to 486 mm 3 (37% decrease). The contralateral lacrimal gland volume decreased from 637 mm 3 to 379 mm 3 (41% decrease). Aqueous tear production increased as well. Schirmer’s test increased by 8.6 mm in the study orbit (59% increase) and 8.7 mm in the fellow orbit (69% increase). The Visual Light Sensitivity Questionnaire-8 (VLSQ-8) score decreased from 18.2 to 6.9 (p < 0.01), demonstrating significant improvement. Mean proptosis measurements in study and fellow orbits were 4.3 mm (p < 0.01) and 2.9 mm (p < 0.01), respectively. In the study, CAS decreased by 4.5 points, from a baseline of 5.0 to 0.6 after treatment (p < 0.01). CAS decreased in fellow orbit by 3.3 points, from 4.0 to 0.8 (p < 0.01). Teprotumumab significantly reduced proptosis and palpebral apertures while increasing tear production; however, no statistical correlation was detected between change in lacrimal gland volume and tear secretion, eyelid height (palpebral aperture), CAS or proptosis. Teprotumumab may directly impact the lacrimal gland and meibomian gland ( ). Parunakian et al . reported similar results ( ). The latter report focused on photosensitivity. Among 90 patients, total mean VLSQ-8 score significantly decreased, including clinically significant improvement (≥2 reduction) in 72 patients (80%). Proptosis and CAS scores improved; however, no correlation was found between light sensitivity and change in CAS or proptosis ( ). These findings suggest that mechanical factors such as corneal exposure may not completely explain lacrimal-related symptoms such as photophobia. Teprotumumab has been recommended as first-line therapy in patients with moderate-severe disease presenting with proptosis and/or diplopia by the American Thyroid Association and European Thyroid Association ( ). The optimal dosing and treatment duration remain uncertain and will require additional clinical trials. Concerns have emerged, both from the RCTs and in clinical experience with teprotumumab, mainly relating to hearing abnormalities and loss (reported in 10% of patients in the two pivotal trials) and worsening of glycemic control (hyperglycemia in 8/84 patients, serum glucose > 160 mg/dL ) ( , ). In addition, the durability of responses has yet to be fully established. Tocilizumab Tocilizumab (TCZ) is a humanized monoclonal antibody, targeting the IL-6 receptor ( , ). TCZ is approved for use in rheumatoid arthritis but has been used off-label for TED. A double-masked RCT with 32 patients was conducted to examine TCZ efficacy in patients with moderate-to-severe corticosteroid-resistant and active TED. CAS improved significantly in the TCZ-treated group. At

In addition, the durability of responses has yet to be fully established. Tocilizumab Tocilizumab (TCZ) is a humanized monoclonal antibody, targeting the IL-6 receptor ( , ). TCZ is approved for use in rheumatoid arthritis but has been used off-label for TED. A double-masked RCT with 32 patients was conducted to examine TCZ efficacy in patients with moderate-to-severe corticosteroid-resistant and active TED. CAS improved significantly in the TCZ-treated group. At week 16, 86.7% vs 35.3% (TCZ-treated vs placebo) of patients had a CAS < 3; however, neither proptosis nor diplopia improved at 40 weeks. Anti-thyroid peroxidase antibody levels were reduced at weeks 16 and 40 compared with baseline, although anti-thyroglobulin antibody (anti-TG), serum TSH, and thyroid stimulating immunoglobulin (TSI) failed to normalize. The adverse events in this study include elevated transaminase levels and acute pyelonephritis. This RCT indicated that TCZ can reduce CAS and inflammation ( ). A meta-analysis of 12 studies (7 prospective, 5 retrospective, and 1 double-masked RCT) reviewed TCZ’s efficacy and safety, and suggested that TCZ treatment might have benefit in TED ( ). Studies in this analysis included those not placebo-controlled, making any conclusions tentative. TCZ must be evaluated further in larger placebo-controlled RCTs that include unselected patient populations ( , ). Thus, while preliminary results appear promising, more evidence about the effectiveness and safety of TCZ in TED is necessary. Rituximab Rituximab (RTX) is a chimeric mouse-human monoclonal antibody that targets the CD20 antigen on B-lymphocytes resulting in their depletion ( – ). Improvement by RTX has been limited to CAS reduction. Evidence concerning its efficacy remains inconsistent and many patients experience adverse events ( , – ). Thus, more evidence is necessary for RTX’s efficacy and safety to be unambiguously determined. Azathioprine Azathioprine (AZA), a DNA synthesis inhibitor ( – ), has been considered an adjuvant therapy. Results suggest its potential in reducing CAS and improving diplopia although this evidence has marginal value ( – ). AZA is associated with major side effects, such as bone marrow suppression, hepatic toxicity, and pancreatitis ( – ). Mycophenolate Mofetil Mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) is the precursor of the immunosuppressive agent, mycophenolic acid (MPA), used widely in organ transplantation and other autoimmune diseases ( , , ). MMF treatment in TED, typically in combination with corticosteroids, is supported by modest evidence ( , ). It is associated with adverse events including gastrointestinal symptoms, elevated transaminases, hypokalemia, and mild liver dysfunction ( , – ). MMF treatment will require stronger evidence demonstrating its efficacy and safety, usually in combination with corticosteroids. Neonatal fragment crystallizable receptor (FcRn) Inhibitors FcRn refers to a class of membrane spanning receptor proteins that are involved in IgG recycling and prolonging their half-life ( ). Batoclimab is a fully human monoclonal antibody that blocks the IgG-binding site on FcRn, thereby facilitating antibody disposal ( ). One proof-of-concept, randomized, and placebo-controlled study found no significant proptosis response to the agent at week 12, although proptosis response was significant at earlier timepoints. Anti-TSHR antibody levels and serum IgG levels decreased also. As a consequence of elevated serum cholesterol levels, that trial was terminated early ( ). Despite the limited study results, Batoclimab and FcRn inhibitors in general represent a potential therapeutic target for TED. Any role for FcRn inhibitors in the TED space will require more robust evidence demonstrating efficacy and safety. IV. Direct Lacrimal System Targeting Treatment Ocular Surface Disease Lacrimal-related symptoms of TED often manifest as ocular surface disease (OSD). Ongoing research suggests that OSD associated with TED results from both anatomical disruption (i.e. proptosis and corneal exposure) and ocular surface inflammation (i.e. tear-film abnormalities and ocular surface cytokines) ( ). First line therapy for OSD and DED includes artificial tears and ointments to supplement tear volume and improve tear film stability. Night-time moisture chambers can be used to maintain hydration and reduce symptomatology of mild TED-related OSD ( , , ). Topical anti-inflammatory agents such as cyclosporine emulsion 0.05% are useful in patients forwhom artificial tears prove insufficient ( , ). Lifitegrast solution is a leukocyte function-associated antigen-1 antagonist approved for DED that can be useful for improving lacrimal symptoms ( ). Secretagogues such as diquafosol and rebamipide stimulate mucin and aqueous secretion while perfluorohexyloctane reduces tear evaporation. Autologous serum tears have also been used ( ). These have been shown to improve tear film stability and reduce symptoms relating to OSD ( ). Contact lenses, including Prosthetic Replacement of the Ocular Surface Ecosystem (PROSE), can be helpful ( – ). V. Surgical Treatments Approaches to surgical rehabilitation for TED depend on the goals of these procedures. They are dictated in part by disease

Secretagogues such as diquafosol and rebamipide stimulate mucin and aqueous secretion while perfluorohexyloctane reduces tear evaporation. Autologous serum tears have also been used ( ). These have been shown to improve tear film stability and reduce symptoms relating to OSD ( ). Contact lenses, including Prosthetic Replacement of the Ocular Surface Ecosystem (PROSE), can be helpful ( – ). V. Surgical Treatments Approaches to surgical rehabilitation for TED depend on the goals of these procedures. They are dictated in part by disease phenotype. In urgent, sight-threatening situations, such as corneal decompensation or dysthyroid optic neuropathy (DON), variable degrees of haste are required. Proptosis and lagophthalmos causing severe eye surface exposure can result in corneal decompensation ( ). Surgical management of DON is typically unrelated to the lacrimal system but the consequences of the surgeries such as orbital decompression can improve globe coverage. Rehabilitative surgeries are indicated for severe, functionally disruptive proptosis that results in corneal exposure ( ). Orbital Decompression Orbital decompression surgery is aimed at expanding the functional orbital volume, accomplished by removal of orbital fat and/or walls of the bony orbit ( , ). The surgical result depends on the extent and anatomical approach used (i.e. number of walls removed, etc.). In so doing, decompression surgery can reduce eyelid retraction. ( , ). Acute orbital decompression is indicated for corneal decompensation and DON. During the inactive disease phase, rehabilitative orbital decompression may be indicated for reducing lacrimal signs and symptoms associated with proptosis, chronic pain/discomfort, and corneal exposure ( ). Eyelid surgery Eyelid repair in TED can involve partial suturing (tarsorrhaphy), or eyelid lengthening. In emergent situations, one of these methods might be employed to manage threatened sight resulting from corneal decompensation ( ). These eyelid procedures can be indicated during either active or chronic, non-progressive TED. In sum, surgery is performed to repair the consequences of proptosis and to protect the cornea ( ). OSD Surgical interventions for the amelioration of OSD target the anatomic underpinnings of accelerated tear evaporation in TED. These procedures include punctal occlusion with punctal plugs or cauterization/destruction ( ), permanent tarsorrhaphy, surgical eyelid retraction correction, amniotic membrane grafting and ocular surface reconstruction ( , ). Botulinum toxin injection (BTX) can be performed as a non-surgical method for lessening upper eyelid retraction. A recent meta-analysis concluded that BTX treatment is effective and well-tolerated, lasting between 1 to 6 months ( ). The side effects included ptosis (13%) and diplopia (2%). These findings are supported by another study assessing BTX in active TED ( ). A recent RCT combined BTX and triamcinolone injections; the results demonstrated more rapid eyelid responses, reduced total triamcinolone dosing, and fewer IOP elevations ( ). BTX is thus a potential alternative to surgical interventions during the active phase of TED. VI. Nonmedical interventions A. Lifestyle Modifications Smoking Cessation Numerous studies have shown an association between cigarette smoking and development or worsening of TED ( , ). A recent meta-analysis confirms evidence supporting this relationship. In that analysis, patients with TED were more likely to be older and actively smoking than patients without TED. Further, patients with active TED were more likely to be current smokers ( ). Both current and past tobacco smoking were associated with increased risk of developing TED. The 2021 EUGOGO guidelines recommend smoking cessation ( ). Thus, patients should be made aware of the risks associated with smoking. They should be referred to experts in smoking cessation. A retrospective cohort study found that 42.4% of individuals achieved smoking cessation and 30.3% of individuals decreased their smoking habit when provided with adequate counselling ( ). Patient Education Patients with TED should be encouraged to play an active role in managing their disease. Educating patients about the nature of their disease and how to optimize its outcome are important. In one study, 21% of patients with TED and 33% of those with thyroidal GD were unaware that tobacco smoking was associated with more severe TED ( ). Moreover, only 50 % and 40% of patients with TED and GD, respectively, were aware that TED is not only associated with hyperthyroidism but can also occur in euthyroid or hypothyroid individuals ( ). All too frequently, the correct diagnosis of TED is delayed. This delay could be attributed to poorly informed doctors and patients ( – ). The lacrimal signs and symptoms (i.e. dry eye, grittiness, etc.) frequently associated with TED can be mistaken for seasonal allergies and other causes of ocular inflammation. Edmunds et al. have advocated enhancing awareness of TED with surveys and questionnaires ( ). Multidisciplinary Care The multisystemic nature of GD, including TED, makes a collaboration between endocrinologists and ophthalmologists necessary to achieve optimal management ( ).

This delay could be attributed to poorly informed doctors and patients ( – ). The lacrimal signs and symptoms (i.e. dry eye, grittiness, etc.) frequently associated with TED can be mistaken for seasonal allergies and other causes of ocular inflammation. Edmunds et al. have advocated enhancing awareness of TED with surveys and questionnaires ( ). Multidisciplinary Care The multisystemic nature of GD, including TED, makes a collaboration between endocrinologists and ophthalmologists necessary to achieve optimal management ( ). Sight-threatening TED should be immediately referred to an oculoplastic surgeon for the prompt evaluation and necessary treatment aimed at vision preservation. A comprehensive eye exam should be conducted at the initial presentation of every patient. Conclusions/Perspectives The lacrimal system is frequently involved in TED. Treatment of thyroid dysfunction is essential to optimize the best possible disease outcomes; however normalizing thyroid function alone represents inadequate treatment for clinically significant TED. Local measures, including preserving the ocular surface and minimizing exposure frequently suffice in mild disease. Medical and surgical remediation might be necessary in more severe disease. Lacrimal symptoms can be associated with among the most emotionally and physically burdensome intrusions in the lives of patients with TED. Teprotumumab, currently the only approved medication for the treatment of TED, can substantially reduce disease activity and severity and provide meaningful relief from lacrimal system-related signs and symptoms. Collaboration between endocrinologists and ophthalmologists should facilitate optimal disease management.

documents.title: EUGOGO clinical activity score and severity assessment of thyroid eye disease

chunks.content: What has changed in thyroid eye disease in the last five years (2020-2025). Significant progress has been made in the management of thyroid eye disease (TED), based on the elucidation of important pathogenic mechanisms. This has led to novel therapeutics validated in randomized clinical trials. Autoreactive antigens that elicit specific orbital immune reactions have not yet been identified, although it has been shown that fibrocytes, circulating stem cells that differentiate into fibroblasts, are expressing the thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor (TSHR) and insulin-like growth factor-1 receptor (IGF-1R) and may be stimulated in the orbit by a cascade of inflammatory reactions inducing adipogenesis. Moderate-severe forms of TED are the target for immunosuppressive therapy. Improvement in the assessment of the active and progressive phase of disease is becoming compelling, as the outcome of a treatment depends on how early during the progressive phase the disease is treated. The clinical activity score may not always help define the right time for treating. In 2020, teprotumumab, an anti-IGF-1 receptor blocker, has been approved by FDA for the treatment of TED. Since then, other drugs were studied or are under investigation and will seek regulatory approval. A series of studies have investigated the role of microbiome in thyroid autoimmunity and TED more in detail, based on the observation that treatment with antibiotics may modify the disease phenotype in a murine model of TED. This approach is being studied for the assessment of TED, especially trying to standardize the use of orbital and facial images for improving the diagnosis of the disease in the early, progressive phase. In the future, these applications will allow the use of synthetic data, in addition to training on real patient images and data.
